summary: Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA) is a fast reroute method for Segment Routing. It precomputes backup paths so traffic can be switched quickly around a failed link or node, protecting node and adjacency segments. It builds on earlier IP fast reroute ideas such as LFA and remote LFA.

plainLanguage.summary: Fast reroute is the practice of moving traffic to a backup path the moment a link or router fails, instead of waiting for the routing protocol to recalculate. This RFC defines a way to do that with Segment Routing, where the backup path is built from segment identifiers that are already in the routing database.

questions: what is the post-convergence path in fast reroute
how does ti-lfa build the repair list
subtitle: Precomputed backup paths for Segment Routing that follow where traffic is expected to go once the network reconverges.

tldr.problem: When a link or router fails, traffic has to be moved to a backup path before the routing protocol has finished recalculating. The existing methods, such as LFA and remote LFA, cannot cover every topology and depend on tunnels or extra protocol sessions.
tldr.mechanism: Each router pre-computes a repair list for every destination, built from the segment identifiers already in the link-state database, so that the backup path follows the path the network is expected to take after the failure. The list is loop-free whatever the forwarding tables of the intermediate routers hold.
tldr.outcome: Protection covers any two-connected network without tunnels or extra sessions, and the backup path matches the post-convergence path, so fewer local policies are needed to choose between backup options.

sections.title: What TI-LFA Does
sections.content:
The document describes a local repair mechanism that uses Segment Routing to restore connectivity when a directly connected component fails. It is designed for link-state Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) shortest path scenarios; non-SR repair mechanisms and non-local failures are out of scope.

The name Topology Independent (TI) describes the capability of providing a loop-free backup path that works across all network topologies. That is the main improvement over LFA, described in RFC 5286, and remote LFA, described in RFC 7490, neither of which can give complete coverage in some topologies, as shown in RFC 6571.

The mechanism works locally at the Point of Local Repair (PLR), the router that detects the failure in one of its own links. Because of that, it does not influence the micro-loops that may form during distributed IGP convergence, or the ones that may form when the failed link comes back. TI-LFA paths are activated from the instant the PLR detects the failure and remain in effect until convergence is complete at the PLR, so they are not susceptible to the micro-loops caused by different convergence times at different nodes. The RFC notes one exception: an early convergence at the PLR followed by an early release of the TI-LFA paths may cause micro-loops, particularly when the paths were computed by the methods in Sections 5.2, 5.3 or 5.4, and that a local convergence delay is one way to prevent this.

For each destination, TI-LFA pre-installs a backup forwarding entry ready for use when a link used to reach that destination fails. It covers a single link failure, a single node failure, or a single Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) failure. Only resources inside a link-state IGP area are protected; protecting exit routers or links attached to another routing domain is out of scope. Using Segment Routing also removes the need for Targeted Label Distribution Protocol sessions with remote nodes, since all the SIDs needed are already in the link-state database, and removes the need for extra state and extra protocol sessions used only to enforce explicit fast reroute paths.
sections.plainLanguage: When a link or router fails, the router next to the failure moves the traffic to a backup path straight away, rather than waiting for every router to work out new routes. This RFC describes how to build those backup paths out of segment identifiers.

sections.title: P-Space, Q-Space and the Repair List
sections.content:
The document defines the terms it uses. The terms old and new topology refer to the state of the link-state database before and after the failure being considered. SPT_old(R) is the shortest path tree rooted at node R in the initial state, and SPT_new(R, X) is the tree rooted at R after resource X has failed. The PLR is the router that restores traffic after detecting a failure in a directly attached link, set of links, or node.

The P-space P(R, X) of a router R with regard to a resource X, such as a link, a node or an SRLG, is the set of routers reachable from R using the pre-convergence shortest paths without any of those paths, including equal-cost path splits, transiting through X. A node in that set is a P node. The extended P-space P'(R, X) is the union of the P-spaces of the neighbours of R that are not themselves reachable from R using X.

The Q-space Q(R, X) is the set of routers from which R can be reached without any path, including equal-cost path splits, transiting through X. A node in that set is a Q node. EP(P, Q) denotes an explicit Segment Routing path from a node P to a node Q.

The primary interface and primary outgoing interface are the outgoing interfaces towards a destination according to the link-state protocol, and the primary link is the link connected to the primary interface. The Adj-SID(S-F) is the adjacency segment from node S to node F.
sections.plainLanguage: Two sets of routers matter. The P-space holds the routers that can still be reached without going through the failed resource. The Q-space holds the routers that can still reach this router without going through it. A repair path joins a router in the first set to a router in the second.

sections.title: The Base Principle
sections.content:
The basic algorithm is to pre-compute SPT_new(R, X) and, for each destination, encode the repair path as a loop-free segment list. One way to get a loop-free list is to use adjacency SIDs only, but that can create very long SID lists that hardware cannot handle because of Maximum SID Depth limits.

An implementation is free to use any local optimisation to produce shorter lists by combining node SIDs and adjacency SIDs. Using node SIDs also allows equal-cost paths to be maximised over the backup path. Those optimisations are out of scope for the document, but the later sections give guidance on using the P-space and Q-space properties to keep the segment list short.

The repair path itself is an outgoing interface and a list of segments, the Repair List (RL), to insert on the SR header as the data plane requires. The RL encodes the explicit, and possibly post-convergence, path to the destination that avoids the protected resource X. It is guaranteed to be loop-free regardless of the state of the forwarding tables along the nodes on the explicit path, as long as those tables are programmed according to a link-state IGP. Because of that guarantee, no coordination or message exchange is needed between the PLR and any other router in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The backup path is a list of segments computed before anything breaks. The list is guaranteed not to loop, whatever the intermediate routers are forwarding at the time, because it is built from the same link-state information they all use.

sections.title: Finding the P and Q Nodes
sections.content:
The challenge in defining a Segment Routing path that follows the expected post-convergence path is keeping the segment list short. To do that, an implementation may determine the P-space, extended P-space and Q-space properties of the nodes along the expected post-convergence path from the PLR to the protected destination, and compute an explicit Segment Routing path from P to Q when the two are not adjacent.

For the extended P-space property, the goal is to find which nodes on the post-convergence path from the PLR R to the destination D are in the extended P-space of R with regard to resource X, where X may be a link, a set of links adjacent to the PLR, or a neighbour node of the PLR. This is done by excluding neighbours that are not on the post-convergence path when computing P'(R, X), and then intersecting the set of nodes on the post-convergence path from R to D with P'(R, X).

For the Q-space property, the goal is to find which nodes on the post-convergence path from R to D are in the Q-space of the destination D with regard to resource X. This is done by intersecting the set of nodes on the post-convergence path with Q(D, X).

RFC 7490 raises scaling concerns about computing a Q-space per destination. The same concerns apply to TI-LFA if an implementation computes a reverse shortest path tree for every destination in the network to determine the Q-space, and it is left to each implementation to choose the right trade-off between scaling and accuracy.
sections.plainLanguage: The repair path is built by finding where the post-convergence path crosses two sets: the routers that can still be reached without the failed resource, and the routers that can still reach the destination without it. The RFC warns that working out the second set for every destination can be expensive.

sections.title: The Four Forms of Repair Path
sections.content:
The repair path is found by intersecting P(S, X) and Q(D, X) with the post-convergence path to the destination, and computing the explicit path EP(P, Q) from a node P in P(S, X) to a node Q in Q(D, X) when the two are not adjacent along that path. The repair list is generally expressed as (Node-SID(P), EP(P, Q)).

The worked example in the RFC uses a topology in which the backup from S to D is computed for the failure of node N1. P(S, N1) is computed and gives [N3, N2, R1], and Q(D, N1) gives [R3]. The expected post-convergence path from S to D with N1 failed is N2, R1, R2, R3, D. The intersection of P(S, N1) with that path is [N2, R1], and the deeper downstream node R1 is used as the P node, while the intersection of Q(D, N1) with the path is [R3], so R3 is the Q node. An explicit path is then computed from R1 to R3 along the post-convergence path, giving the adjacency segments Adj-SID(R1-R2) and Adj-SID(R2-R3).

The RFC then describes four common forms. When a direct neighbour is in both P(S, X) and Q(D, X) and the link to it is on the post-convergence path, the outgoing interface is set to that neighbour and the repair segment list is empty; this is comparable to a post-convergence LFA repair. When a remote node R is in both sets and on the post-convergence path, the repair list is a single node segment to R and the outgoing interface is the one used to reach R, comparable to a post-convergence RLFA repair tunnel. When a node P in P(S, X) and a node Q in Q(D, X) are both on the post-convergence path and adjacent to each other, the repair list is two segments, a node segment to P followed by an adjacency segment from P to Q, comparable to a post-convergence DLFA repair tunnel. In other cases there is no adjacent P and Q node along the post-convergence path, and a list of adjacency SIDs can encode the path between them, though the PLR may compute a shorter list, which is left to the implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four shapes the backup path can take. It can be empty, when a neighbour can still reach the destination. It can be a single node segment. It can be a node segment followed by one adjacency segment. And it can be a longer list of segments that the implementation computes for itself.

sections.title: Repair Lists for Node and Adjacency Segments
sections.content:
These procedures work the same way for the Segment Routing over MPLS and the Segment Routing over IPv6 data planes. They describe how a protecting router S handles the active segment of a packet when its primary outgoing interface for that packet, the S-F link, fails.

When the active segment is a node segment, the active segment must be kept on the SR header unchanged and the repair list must be added. The active segment then becomes the first segment after the repair list, and the way the list is added depends on the data plane.

When the active segment is an adjacency segment S-F, the simplest approach for link protection is to create a repair list that carries the traffic to F. This is done with one or more PUSH operations. If the repair list, while avoiding S-F, terminates on F, S pushes only the segments of the repair list. Otherwise S pushes a node segment of F followed by the segments of the repair list. This method merges the traffic back at the remote end of the adjacency segment and keeps as much traffic as possible on the pre-failure path, but where SR policies are in use and strict compliance with the policy is required, an end-to-end protection should be preferred over this local repair.

Two cases follow. If the next segment in the list is an adjacency segment, S must apply a NEXT operation on Adj-SID(S-F) and then one or more PUSH operations, with the same rule about pushing a node segment of F when the repair list does not end at F. A packet arriving with a segment list matching [adj-sid(S-F), adj-sid(F-M), ...] then leaves S with a list matching [RL(F), node(F), adj-sid(F-M), ...], where RL(F) is the repair list for destination F. If the next segment in the stack is a node segment for node T, S must apply a NEXT operation on the adjacency segment related to S-F, followed by a PUSH of a repair list redirecting the traffic to a node Q whose path to node segment T is not affected by the failure, so the packet leaves S with a list matching [RL(Q), node(T), ...].

The RFC notes a limit of the local repair: when the source node uses Traffic Engineering, the PLR generally cannot know which post-convergence path the source will select, because the computation is local to the source and depends on constraints the PLR may not know, so no method applied at the PLR can guarantee that the protection follows the post-convergence path.
sections.plainLanguage: When the failing link is carrying a node segment, the router adds the backup segments after it. When it is carrying an adjacency segment, the router replaces the failed hop with the backup segments, so the traffic still arrives where it was going.

sections.title: Data Plane and Algorithm Considerations
sections.content:
For the MPLS data plane, described in RFC 8660, two rules apply when creating a repair list. If the active segment is a node segment signalled with penultimate hop popping, and the repair list ends with an adjacency segment terminating on the penultimate node of the active segment, then the active segment must be popped before the repair list is pushed. If the active segment is a node segment but those conditions are not met, the active segment must be popped and then pushed again with a label value computed according to the Segment Routing Global Block of the endpoint of the repair list, and the repair list must then be pushed.

For the SRv6 data plane, described in RFC 8754 and RFC 8986, the path computation algorithm is the same. Adjacency SIDs are typically globally routed there, so there is no need to precede an adjacency SID with a prefix SID and the resulting repair list is likely shorter. When traffic is protected at a transit node, an SRv6 SID list is added to the packet to apply the repair list, following the head-end behaviours. When traffic is protected at an SR Segment Endpoint Node, the segment endpoint packet processing runs first, and the packet is then protected as if it were a transit packet.

Section 8 of the RFC relates TI-LFA to the SR algorithms. An operator can bind an algorithm to a prefix SID, and the default algorithm is the Shortest Path algorithm, which an operator can override with local policies. When TI-LFA uses node SIDs associated with the default algorithm, there is no guarantee that the path will be loop-free, because a local policy may have overridden the expected IGP path; making sure the deployed policies do not interfere becomes the operator's responsibility, and the RFC notes that the same situation already arises with existing mechanisms such as RLFA.

RFC 9350 defines the Flexible Algorithm framework, which associates a constrained path with a prefix SID. An implementation may support TI-LFA for node SIDs bound to a Flexible Algorithm. In that case it should use the constrained shortest path algorithm bound to the Flexible Algorithm, instead of the regular Dijkstra, in all the shortest path and reverse shortest path computations carried out during the TI-LFA computation, including the P-space, the Q-space and the post-convergence path. It should also build the repair list only from node SIDs and adjacency SIDs bound to the Flexible Algorithm, or from unprotected adjacency SIDs of the regular shortest path.
sections.plainLanguage: The same backup list is used whether the network runs Segment Routing over MPLS or over IPv6, with small differences in how the labels are handled. If the operator has bound a different algorithm to a prefix, the backup path must be computed with that algorithm, or the traffic will not follow the constraints the operator asked for.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The techniques in this document are internal functions of a router. They bound the time taken to restore traffic after a directly connected link or node fails, and because they steer traffic to the post-convergence path as quickly as possible they reduce the disruption caused by a local failure, which the RFC describes as a modest security enhancement. The protection mechanism does not protect external destinations; it restores traffic to destinations inside the routing domain.

The security considerations of RFC 5286 and RFC 7490 apply, as do the considerations for Segment Routing itself in RFC 8402 and for its data plane instantiations in RFC 8660, RFC 8754 and RFC 8986. The document introduces no additional security concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is exposed by this mechanism. It restores traffic inside the routing domain faster after a local failure, and everything else about its security comes from the fast reroute and Segment Routing documents it builds on.

viz.caption: The terms the repair path computation uses

items.title: Point of Local Repair
items.text: The router that restores traffic after detecting a failure in a directly attached link, set of links or node.

items.title: P-space
items.text: The routers reachable from a router along the pre-convergence shortest paths, without any of those paths passing through the failed resource.

items.title: Extended P-space
items.text: The union of the P-spaces of the neighbours that are not themselves reachable through the failed resource.

items.title: Q-space
items.text: The routers from which a router can be reached without any path, including equal-cost splits, passing through the failed resource.

items.title: Repair List
items.text: The list of segments the PLR inserts on the SR header to carry the traffic to the destination.

items.title: Post-convergence path
items.text: The path traffic is expected to take once the IGP has converged after the failure.

viz.caption: What makes the backup path loop-free

items.title: Computed before the failure
items.text: The repair list is pre-computed and pre-installed for every destination, ready for the moment the failure is detected.

items.title: Built from the link-state database
items.text: The segments used are already in the link-state database, so no extra protocol sessions with remote routers are needed.

items.title: Loop-free whatever the tables hold
items.text: The list stays loop-free regardless of the forwarding tables of the nodes on the path, as long as they are programmed from a link-state IGP.

items.title: No coordination needed
items.text: Because of that guarantee, the repairing router does not have to exchange messages with any other router before it switches the traffic over.

items.title: Active segment is a node segment
items.text: The active segment stays on the header unchanged and the repair list is added after it.

items.title: Next segment is an adjacency segment
items.text: The router applies NEXT on the failed adjacency segment, then pushes the repair list, adding a node segment for the far end when the list does not end there.

items.title: Next segment is a node segment
items.text: The router applies NEXT on the failed adjacency segment, then pushes a repair list that redirects the traffic to a node whose onward path is unaffected.
